ety.text: From Middle English eche, elche, ilch, from Old English ǣlċ, contraction of ǣġhwelċ. Comparable to aye + alike. Compare Scots ilk, elk (“each, every”), Saterland Frisian älk (“each”), West Frisian elk, elts (“each”), Dutch elk (“each”), Low German elk, ellik (“each”), German Low German elk, elke (“each, every”), German jeglicher (“any”). By surface analysis, Old English ā + which.

senses.d: All; every; qualifying a singular noun, indicating all examples of the thing so named seen as individual or separate items (compare every).
ex: Make sure you wash each bowl well.
The sun comes up each morning and sets each night.

senses.d: Individually; separately; used in a sentence with a plural subject to indicate that the action or state described by the verb applies to all members of the described group individually, rather than collectively to the entire group.
ex: We ordered half a chicken each, but we each got a whole one.
You are each right in a different way.

senses.d: Every one/thing individually or one by one.
ex: I'm going to give each of you a chance to win.
From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs.

senses.d: An individual item: the least quantitative unit in a grouping.
ex: An each, piece, single item, or individual item package.
The commonly used term “each” means that each individual item is one unit.

ety.text: From Middle French chasque, a backformation from chascun, from Old French chascun (whence modern chacun). The Old French derives from a conflation of Vulgar Latin *quiscunus (from quisque unus) with synonymous *catunus (from cata unus, from Ancient Greek κατά (katá), whence Catalan, Spanish, and Portuguese cada).

Inherited from Old Italian onne~onni (with /ˈɔ-/ per the Latin etymon), from Latin omnis. The development of palatalized /-ɲ-/ and closed /ˈo-/, already attested in the thirteenth century (ógne, later ógni), are due to the word being frequently unstressed.
From Vulgar Latin *cisque-unus, from Latin quisque ūnus, and influenced by cadauno. Cf. French chacun, Catalan cadascun.

Ancient Greek κατά (katá)bor. Latin cata Old Spanish cada Spanish cada Inherited from Old Spanish cada, from Latin cata, borrowed from Ancient Greek κατά (katá), from Proto-Hellenic *kətá, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥-th₂, from *ḱóm, possibly from *ḱe. Compare English catalogue.
Cf. Old Spanish cadauno, from Latin cata (< Ancient Greek κατά (katá)) + unum. Compare Occitan cadun, Catalan cadascun; cf. French chacun.

Inherited from Old Spanish seños, sennos, sendos (first attested in Cantar de mio Cid, via an intermediary *senlos (see coyunda for a similar development), from Latin singulus. Compare with sencillo which was inherited via a diminutive of the same Latin root.

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese cada, from Latin cata (“by”), from Ancient Greek κατά (katá).

Inherited from Middle French chascun, from Old French chascun, from Vulgar Latin *cascunum, *casquunum, a conflation of quisque unum (“each one”) + *cata unum, a variant form showing a derivative of Ancient Greek κατά (katá) (this variant form survived into Old French as chaün).
